[h1]In-Depth[/h1]
[h3]Setting & Writing[/h3]
In an alternate timeline, the USSR has become a technological powerhouse after WW2, with breakthroughs in fields such as nanotechnology, AI and energy manipulation that far surpass those of our present-day world. Affirming itself as the leading world power, it builds the utopian symbol-city of Chelomey, and nears the launch of Kollektiv 2.0, a worldwide neural network merging man and machine to an unprecedented degree. Agent P-3, the protagonist, attends the ceremony, but things take a horribly wrong turn.

The narrative shines the most in its indirect form, through the visual clues and remains from events transpired before, while it proves mediocre in both lore files, dialogues and cutscenes. The worst offender is your musclehead alter-ego, which not only has the intellectual capacity of a broken treadmill, but is also a ceaseless discharge of cringe, with puns and lines that make Leon from RE4 seem like Socrates. The events are predictable, moral dilemmas get sidetracked, and the classic rushed exposition dump near the end comes as the last nail in this atomic coffin.

[h3]Exploration & Secrets[/h3]
The world is divided between linear and open-world areas, the latter becoming available only several hours later. The sprawl of facilities, complexes and residential areas comprising the freely roamed, although a few may be inaccessible until a specific story point is reached. In both instances, minutely exploring with the aid of your Scanner tool to highlight loot and other important things, will be paramount to accumulate crafting supplies, blueprints and useful consumables, while also discovering files and secret areas from time to time. 

It’s satisfying and enjoyable to traverse the world by foot or car - no fast travel so make sure you search accurately. Save points are placed regularly, allowing you to use them unlimited times. The main difference between closed and open-world areas is the enemy presence, much more massive outside, featuring reinforcements and an alarm level system, although your foes can be temporarily disabled by destroying a certain facility.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2944133332

[h3]Combat System & Bosses[/h3]
With firearms, improvised melee tools and polymer-based powers at his disposal, P-3 is a living arsenal. Your limited, upgradable inventory can hold a generous amount of ammo, weapons and consumables to keep you alive in a fight, while powers and abilities only have cooldowns, no other resource than time is required. Energy is used instead to power certain weapons, and is gained passively, with consumables or by striking foes in melee. A dodge system allows you to avoid melee and ranged hits, while defensive upgrades and medkits do the rest. 

Enemies range from simple humanoid bots to mechanical horrors with many weapons and moves, and dangerous mutants worthy of STALKER’s Zone. Mini and proper bosses are uncommon sights, giving you fights that won’t prove too tough especially later on, due to your arsenal becoming way too powerful, same for your skills, granting you simply too many advantages for these fights to be as ‘epic’ as they should be. Unless you get caught in an insta-kill QTE - those are crap.

[h3]Character Progression & Crafting System[/h3]
AI-powered fridges, sometimes considerably more horny than expected, will be at your service to craft all sorts of consumables, ammo and upgrade both your weapons and P-3’s abilities -provided you have the needed materials, blueprints and XP, all looted from the world and enemies. These upgrades will add secondary fire modes to guns, improve their stats, specialize them to damage other robots or organics, and upgrade all of your abilities to be stronger, faster, and last longer.

In general, provided you loot thoroughly, you will never run out of anything and be in far excess of materials to make all the ammo, health kits and other stuff you may need. It has to be noted that scrapping weapons or abilities returns 100% of their materials, so that you can try different ones and spice up the gameplay, a good choice that however hinders the replay value, since you can “have it all” in the same playthrough this way.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2944380105

[h3]Puzzles & Optional Content[/h3]
Both linear and open sections feature a generous quantity of puzzles, that range from logic-based locks, to timing sequences, beam redirections, and more than a few unique ones with their own mechanics. None of them is very complex, and they’re accessible even to those who aren’t familiar with the puzzle genre. Testing Grounds (dungeons) are the main secondary content, awarding unique upgrades for weapons and requiring some extra effort to unlock.
Wait...Hold on....they, they actually did it! Someone developed a game that's actually OPTIMIZED on launch? Surely this must be a dream.......

Definitely not what I expected. I thought this was gonna be some serious sci-fi hardcore survivor game based around a story, but instead got a sci-fi fever dream. Atomic Heart seems to take inspiration from a lot of familiar titles like Fallout for it's world design, a mix of Bioshock and Dead Island for its game play and freaking Looney Tunes for it's story.  This game's story is probably the most psychotic thing I've had to experience in the past 10 years. 

The gameplay is a tier above basic FPS, allowing you to use as many weapons as you can carry with 3 alternate special powers that try to work in tandem with one another. The games default difficulty could be hard enough to justify all that, I typically just used my best one and had so much ammo for every gun I settled for just blasting. 

My biggest gripe with this game overall was it's dialogue in English. Specifically in English, cause there are parts of this game where the translation feels like it was totally 1 to 1 with its original language, creating these very rushed feeling cut scenes with dialogue cutting itself off, almost as if 2 people couldn't talk at the same time. It was just awkward overall. As for the dialogue content, I think a lot of people will be split on this but the main character in English and some other characters are very colorful I'd say. A lot of what the main character says or does is very wacky and his glove companion don't really seem to mesh well with him. It's like if a high ranking officer in the military acted like a neurodivergent teen that watches My Little Pony on his adventures with his milquetoast robot butler. On the other hand, I think the main character made more fun, he's just largely immature. 

Also the PC version was insanely smooth for a Denuvo user, only thing that was suspicious was how long the loading elevators were. But I kept 144 in the open world very consistently with no stuttering. I even tried to get a whole village to attack me and it barely dropped.

 [h3]All in all its more than worth grabbing,[/h3] Its on sale quite a bit these days, ($26 CAN as I'm writing this) and for that price, I think people need to take a chance on this and make up their own minds whether its fun for them.

Atomic Heart plays something like a mix between BioShock and Half-Life. While some aspects of the game are genius, others feel bafflingly amateurish.

On one hand you have the presentation. Mundfish takes some big swings and most of them connect. The visuals impress, both on a technical and design level. Environments and set pieces are detailed and often impressively creative. The sound also deserves mention. Music is eclectic, but the quality undeniable. You won't like every piece, but you're sure to love some of them.

On the other hand, you have the gameplay. Endlessly spawning, self-repairing enemies. Dull, tedious fetch quests and puzzles. Repeatedly entering/exiting different menus and rewatching long-winded animations. Several times I asked myself: "Am I doing this right? Is this really how I'm supposed to play?"

Despite introducing a lot of cool high-level sf concepts, the story somehow manages to feel quite uninteresting. It's also laughably contrived. [spoiler]Throughout the story, basically every named character is revealed to be working for the opposite side.[/spoiler] I also found the tone a little strange, it definitely feels like something was lost in translation (and the English dub doesn't help).

A severely flawed but commendably bold and ambitious game. A unique experience. Weakest of recommends.

This is a unique but somewhat flawed game. It feels very much like a cross between Bioshock and Soviet Wolfenstein The New Collosus, and that's really cool. The overall world building of the game is incredibly novel, and the presentation is very well done. Where this game excells, it feels like game of the year material. Unfortunately, there are elements in the game which are a lot less brilliant, and these aspects pull the whole experience down from glowing greatness to just good.

One major flaw in the game is the writing. While the world building itself is great, and the overall story is pretty good, the dialogue that carries the story often feels annoying, mostly because of the protagonist, who is a huge whiner. Throughout the game, he doesn't stop complaining about how everything sucks, and that clashes with your own experience of being pretty impressed with the world and wanting to enjoy it. To be fair, the Russian version of the dialogue is better, so it is definitely a fault of translation. Russian cursing has a lot of subtleties in tone and context which the English language doesn’t have (I sometimes like to joke that a true master of the Russian language knows how to curse politely), and all of those nuances are homogenized into a unidimensional tone that often sounds whiny in English. Since most people will probably play this in English, the issue stands, even though the original script is obviously not this flawed.
For the same reason of cultural tone lost in translation, some of the attempts at humor end up being quite obnoxious, like that horny upgrades machine that is a lot more tame in Russian, but goes full cringe in the English version.

Another major problem that spoils the game is the combat, which feels a bit like a chore. The weapons feel underpowered, the reload animations are long, and the enemies constantly knock you down. Overall, the combat is actually reasonably balanced, it's just annoying that the balanced experience is one of you fighting big waves of enemies while constantly being held back by the shooting mechanics, where nothing feels powerful, and things like getting up from a knockdown or reloading feel slow. I played it on the medium difficulty, thinking it's the "regular" difficulty, and it actually feels like the hard difficulty. Playing it on easy is such a better experience, and feels like most other shooters.

There were times when I was hoping to avoid battle using some stealth, but there's pretty much no stealth mechanics in this game. Aside from crawl-sneaking behind an enemy when they are not looking, or keeping a large enough distance, there's no way to pass enemies unnoticed. If you try to hide behind bushes, they'll see you anyway.

In conclusion, the game has great world building and pretty cool level design, as well as fantastic graphics, and a lot of Russian charm, but is dragged down by annoying dialogue and tedious combat. Both are fixable if you play on easy and use the Russian voice acting.

If you hate the english voice actor there's something you need to understand.

[h1]  Atomic Heart: Variety in the Service of Creativity [/h1]

[b] Foreword [/b]

I enjoy reading the various reviews on Steam, and AH is, of course, already the subject of many.

However, I’d like to point out that, whether the review is positive or negative, it’s important to realise that people with less than 4–5 hours on the clock won’t have seen the game at all. That’s the average time it takes to get through the introductory phase to the actual game and its mechanics, and whilst this gives a first impression of AH in general, players are missing out on almost all of the content.

You’ve been warned.

[b] STORY [/b]

The story of AH is relatively interesting. Without giving anything away, the setting and plot are really gripping. It’s quite well portrayed and presented, and the characters have a real presence (perhaps a little too much so). The stakes are clear, and honestly, it’s hard not to want to carry on.

I still haven’t finished the story, but I can’t wait to find out more. I’ll update this review if things change.

AH’s big problem isn’t its storyline or its world. Nor is it the writing in general. No, the BIG problem… is the dialogue. It’s all written (and voiced) absolutely terribly. It’s very strange, actually. As for the French dub, it sounds as though it was done in two stages. Some dialogue is convincing, even if it’s a bit silly, whilst other bits are completely off the mark in terms of intonation and so on. It’s as if certain lines were added in a rush afterwards. Really, only the Russian dub is properly worth listening to, even though the French dub isn’t actually that bad.

Overall, it’s a far cry from the standard set by *Forespoken*, but it’s still surprising.
 
Where the game really shines, however, is in everything else. The visual storytelling, the world-building, the lore, the coherence of the universe – EVERYTHING is fascinating, and for anyone with even a passing interest in dystopian fiction or even the Soviet era, it’s a real treat; everything is inspired, and almost everything carries symbolic meaning – it’s really well put together. You can tell the team have put in a lot of time and effort, and the whole project oozes the developers’ passion.


For the more curious among you, you can really see the remnants of the film that AH was originally meant to be. If you’re already familiar with the concept art, videos and everything else that’s been released since 2008, you’ll be pleasantly surprised to delve into the developers’ creative minds...

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2937173926

[b] GAMEPLAY [/b]

I’ve seen a few lost souls criticising the core gameplay and the gunplay, and I really struggle to understand why. Admittedly, the FOV is quite narrow and this quickly makes everything feel a bit odd, but it doesn’t detract from the game in any way.

The weapons (melee or ranged) are fun and responsive; the guns pack a punch and you really know how to use them depending on the situation. The enemies are varied and each has their own resistances and weaknesses, which forces the player to be a bit versatile. Similarly, not all enemies are revealed straight away, so you don’t necessarily have time to get bored with enemy number one, as you very quickly discover others as you progress.

Aside from combat, there’s also platforming and puzzles. Whilst not particularly original, the game manages to feel refreshing. For example, the lock-picking mechanics are quite varied (three or four different types) and original enough to surprise you. This, once again, prevents boredom from constantly repeating the exact same animation or QTE. The puzzles are also varied, and although they inevitably often follow the same basic principle, they’re quite enjoyable and often serve as a gimmick within the ‘dungeons’.

The dungeons, incidentally – referred to here as ‘test sites’ – are in fact dungeons, instances that allow you to collect blueprints to upgrade your weapons. These sites are often blocked by a puzzle on the surface and offer a few minutes of pure joy (yes, really). They allow the game to make the most of its puzzle mechanics and let you take down a few mobs, even including bosses!
 
On the face of it, the map turns out to be a reasonable size (it’s not exactly *The Witcher 3* either). The various locations aren’t that far apart, and exploring the map is a pleasure. There isn’t much to do apart from travelling between the different locations, looting or collecting secrets, and talking to corpses (yes, really – twice). The good news is that the game doesn’t fall into the usual open-world pitfalls, and once again it manages to feel refreshing in that respect.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2936834888

[b] GRAPHICS AND OPTIMISATION [/b]

Graphically, the game looks stunning. There’s one MAJOR downside, though: the game doesn’t support RTX. In itself, this wouldn’t be a problem if the game hadn’t been so heavily marketed specifically for its RTX capabilities… And it’s clear the game was designed with RTX in mind; between the lighting and reflective surfaces, I’m just desperate for the RTX patch to arrive.

Apart from that, the game looks absolutely stunning. At the risk of repeating myself, the developers’ creativity is incredible and the attention to detail is truly meticulous.

As surprising as it may seem, the game runs like a dream. Yes! It’s missing RTX, but a UE4 game is well optimised – hooray!

It looks great, it runs smoothly – is there a problem or not?

Not in itself, but there are QUITE A FEW things missing: RTX, photo mode, HUD options, FOV settings and possibly a few extra graphics options. It remains to be seen what content will be added over time.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2936732710

[b] CONCLUSION [/b]

I highly recommend Atomic Heart. For a project that’s been in the works since 2008, it more than lives up to its promises. The world is coherent, the game is fun, and the story is interesting. The game is far from being a masterpiece, nor even a Game of the Year contender, but it deserves credit for seeing its ideas through to the end and offering an experience that, whilst not entirely original, is at least refreshing!

PS: The game doesn’t suffer from major bugs or optimisation issues, but it’s clear that some aspects aren’t quite polished. A few minor bugs can detract from the experience or prevent you from progressing. At the time of writing, an update to the Game Pass version is preventing players from loading their save files.

This is a very difficult game to review. It has some really awesome moments and a lot of annoyances and weird stuff.
Played on Armageddon difficulty.

[h2]Main game[/h2]
[h3]Pros[/h3]
- Visuals are fantastic and work perfectly in tandem with music to create the high-tech alternate soviet reality. Music is especially good, some oldies, some metal covers of them, some modern music too - all work great in creating the mood and it even has lore explanation as to why there is music from the future. Atomic Heart is something in-between Prey and Bioshock gameplay wise.
- There are "portal"-like dungeons with puzzles and good loot that are fun to explore, accompanied by "club" music, which fits well and creates a unique vibe.
- At the time of writing this review there were 2 out of 4 DLCs released and they are important for the lore and story which I enjoyed. Though DLC's gameplay, especially in 
- Atomic heart allows you to change your skills or weapons at a vending machine (Eleonora ;)))) anytime you want with a full refund which is awesome, I wish all games would have this feature, it's nice to experiment and try things out for yourself without the need to follow some guide to avoid choice errors.

[h3]Nuances[/h3]
- Enemies are sponges and there's not enough ammo in the beginning, you MUST use abilities and melee. I got used to it and later in the game was actually shooting more and had a bunch of ammo. Maybe playing on normal difficulty would solve this.
- Enemies are also almost endless in the open world part, which is very annoying. Technically you can disable them for a time, but it's not worth it IMO, better to just move to objective or "run'n'explore" and fight only if necessary.
- I played with Russian voice overs, sometimes it's great and sometimes it's awful, feels like actors weren't instructed properly which emotion the character was suppose to convey, so it has weird moments where the actor shouts and swears, but it's not really necessary and the other way around when char is very calm when the situation is anything but. Main protagonist is a bit of a "brute", but to my surprise it actually has a lore explanation on why he is that way, so that's not a negative.
- The movement is clunky, I often found myself getting stuck during fights in some boxes or other objects while running around. Thank goodness there are some great abilities that can save you in sticky situations like that, so I didn't really die that often because of that.
- Most melee weapons are trash, energy weapons aren't really powerful and are mostly useless except for the basic energy gun.
- A bit too many locked door puzzles, while I did enjoy them in the beginning, by the end of the game they became tedious. There's an option to auto-solve those in accessibility settings, but I didn't use it.

[h3]Cons[/h3]
A bunch of small bugs, for example whenever you pull up to a tight space you always get a split second view through the ceiling, some animations are in "low-fps" weird state, constant achievement pop-up for no reason, enemies/objects getting stuck mid air. Occasional stutters and the shaders are taking too much time to compile at the start of the game. Sometimes script doesn't trigger the necessary events in Annihilation Instinct DLC, so you have to reload or replay.

[h3]Conclusion[/h3]
Having said all that the game isn't bad at all and I actually liked it, but it has many annoyances. I give 7-10 to games I like, so in this case I can't give it anything higher than a 7/10.


[h2]DLC #1 - Annihilation Instinct[/h2]
Main story gives you a major decision at the end of the game and this DLC shows you the non-canon ending and what would happen after it.
Knowing which ending is canon kind of detracts from this DLC's value to be honest and makes it skippable. It's not bad overall, but nothing special.
6/10

[h2]DLC #2 - Trapped in limbo[/h2]
This DLC is very different from the main story. It feels like a mod more than an actual official release, a compilation of experiments that devs probably did for fun while they were drunk having a hackathon in the office. It's wacky, it's silly, but as weird as it is I actually liked it in the end, but it takes some time to "click".
6/10

[h2]DLC #3 - Enchantment Under the Sea[/h2]
Now this is the real deal, this is all I wanted from the game, take everything I wrote in the "nuances" and "cons" section and remove it, devs basically fixed everything I didn't like, your melee weapon is now powerful, the enemies are no longer bullet sponges, no open world infinite spawns, just linear, well paced story. Atomic Heart is perhaps the most unique game I've played in a really long time. I can say with certainty that even though I might have played games where some of the features Atomic heart includes are present, nowhere were they implemented in a way that Atomic Heart has done so. That's not to say that the game is perfect, far from it in fact, but in this case I think saying "imperfection has a beauty of its own" is the right way to describe how I felt after finishing it.

At first I'd like to say that the story is a complete fustercluck. There is no other way of putting it. The characters all sound a bit off (especially the player character) and the dialogue simply isn't the best. Even though I don't think many would aproach Atomic Heart and expect it to be a storytelling masterpiece, it's still an important fact to be made aware of. 

Even though the game has been advertised as an open world game, I don't really think of it as such. And that's not necessarily a bad thing per se. The way I would describe this world is that it's a one giant linear level with optional detours with certain stages where after a certain point the player gets locked out of the place where he can't go back to anymore. At the start I was very confused by this progression but with a little bit of hindsight I appreciate it for what it is. It's just that the advertised description didn't really do this game justice. It's not necessary to make every game into an open world and I think the way Atomic Heart's world has been handled is both unique and effective.

Now to the combat. I cannot describe in words how good, polished, satisfying and rewarding it feels. Even though a lot of the enemies are what could be considered a bullet sponge at first, it all comes together near the end of the game when you have your entire arsenal and are let loose to cause as much havoc and carnage as possible. The way the robots react, the way your special abilities and weapons work together to slowly tear those robots apart, especially when upgraded, it's simply majestic (that also applies to the bossfigths which are also really great even if a little on the simple side in some cases). And all of that is accompanied by an amazing soundtrack. All the people who worked on it have done an amazing job creating something unique, fitting to the aesthetic of Atomic Heart and also sometimes nostalgic for those that remember some of the original classics that were remixed (I'm not one of those people, but I can only imagine what it must feel like to hear a song you've been listening to as a kid on a radio in this game completely remixed while ripping your enemies to pieces).

Let's talk about the visuals. Atomic heart looks pretty good grapics-wise, but the art style completely surpases the level of detail in my opinion. Sure, it might feel a bit schizophrenic the way it shifts constantly to a new theme and visual style all the time, but I found it actually quite fitting for the setting - the utopian Soviet Union. It's simply something that hasn't been done before and we don't really have anything to compare it to other than the real world history of the USSR, where, funnily enough, megalomania, utopian visions and plans for the future were quite common among the elite, not unlike those found in Atomic Heart (albeit with a more realistic visual style). I simply found it incredibly interesting to be interpreted in this way and thorouhgly enjoyed the art style/styles. Oh and let me just mention that the game runs like a dream so you can enjoy all of what is throws at you without worrying about awful fps drops, stutters or crashes (unlike many Unreal engine releases lately).

The final verdict is incredibly straight forward. If you'd like to play a game with great combat, great graphics and awesome soundtrack and you don't care as much about the story, Atomic Heart is a no-brainer. The best way to apporach it is to not compare it to what's already out there. It's not a "Russian Bioshock", or "Russian Fallout" like many would describe it, it's not even an open world game or an RPG in my humble opinion, it's its own thing and I love it for that. Maybe you will as well.

TLDR; 
Wait for it to go on sale or get it on gamepass, just don't pay full price. Very repetitive, a lot of highs, a lot of lows, messy pacing, but enough interesting things to keep you going. Paints both communism and capitalism as bad if you cared about that. There's actually quite a bit of robot girls.

The good:
- The music is definitely the highlight. At its best its really good and exciting, at its worst its still interesting. Which is better than forgettable imo

- Great setting and visuals
- Story is decent, nothing mindblowing. There are a few things that don't make sense, but there is still setup and payoff within the narrative
- I felt the difficulty was fine throughout. I was never on autopilot when in combat and would still find myself making mistakes and dying. There are certain perks that are a must have and you definitely feel the progression. I found myself wanting to avoid combat near the start, but not at all near the end.
- I liked every side character/robot. There was a certain red robot that I wish had more screen time. It was fun whenever I saw it. I've seen that some people HATED this character, but I personally like it.

- Very small and isolated moments throughout the I absolutely loved. Like some character interaction or world building moments. 


The bad:
- Probably the biggest issue: pacing pacing pacing. It made no sense. They tried to do what Bioshock Infinite did with seeing columbia all nice and pretty and happy before things go wrong, except not as well both thematically and in execution. You sit through what is basically an interactive cut scene with really on-the-nose exposition and a lot of NPCs going "wow, it sure is amazing that we have such amazing science in [city name] thanks to [name] and their [invention] that recently came out." After this you, you arrive in the open world to go to the first mission/dungeon. I then spent 4 hours on this first mission. Then back to the open world for 10 minutes to get to the next story mission. Then another 2-3 hours on that. Then everything gets shorter on average afterwards. The first half of the game has so many puzzles that you would think it was a puzzle game first before a FPS, but then the last half of the game has literally no puzzles so idk. Its a mess.
- The game has an "open world" tag, but is only "open world" in that there is an overworld that you can explore (kinda). However, there isn't really anything to do other than collect weapon blueprints and kill robots. The overworld only stands as a set piece to get from story mission to story mission. I spent maybe an 1.5 hours total in the overworld, and I was really trying to find interesting things to do. There was a point in which I wanted to travel to get an upgrade for a weapon only to find that the entire section of the map was cut off and I had to progress through the story to open it. There wasn't even any indication that it opened when it did. And by the time it did, I didn't need the upgrade. The combat cycle for the overworld can just be ignored. There are sometimes just too many enemies in a given location. Like, you will scan the area and there's 30 things on your screen with lines connecting them and then they just keep adding more and more as you progress through the story. 
- There are lines of dialog that are just bad. Not even like "oh that could have been better". More like "I wish i didn't have to listen to that". You kinda get used to it though. Or maybe it just improved a bit over the course of the game
- Voice acting is good, but the direction is often terrible. The MC will say a line and deliver it well, but in a tone and inflection that does not fit the situation at all. I found this happening a lot. I'm told the Russian VA is the best option.
- Unbelievably repetitive. Very little enemy variety. Only (one)? dead soldier model. You will spend hours collecting things to put into other things to open doors and then open some variation of three lock types on a door to again collect things to open another door and then talk to an unmoving dead body. Each time you fight some amount of the 6 or so enemy types. (eidt:I looked this up, there are 9 normal types. 3 have variants. The rest are boss types. You see one type way more than the rest). The game also tries to be cute with it by having the MC say something sarcastic like "Wow, another lock on the door. Who would have seen that coming?", or "Yeah, of course I have to go collect more capsules. What else could it have possibly been?". As though that makes this type of game design excusable. 
- The first boss fight blew my mind away. Like probably the best moment of the game. Then all other boss fights are boring.

Verdict: ⭐⭐⭐ (3/5) – “A visual feast served on a plate of chores.”

Atomic Heart is a rare breed of game: it is simultaneously one of the most imaginative shooters in recent years and one of the most deeply irritating experiences to actually play. It feels like a high-budget Soviet fever dream that was built by geniuses but balanced by people who hate your free time.

The Good: A World Like No Other
Visually, the game is a 10/10. The "Soviet-futurism" aesthetic is breathtaking, blending 1950s utopia with terrifyingly sleek robotics. From the haunting ballerina twins to the booming industrial soundtrack by Mick Gordon, the atmosphere is thick, polished, and genuinely unique. When you are moving through the linear, underground story sections, the game feels like a worthy successor to BioShock.

The Bad: The "Repair Drone" Nightmare
The moment you step into the open world, the game’s "chore" factor skyrockets. The core mechanic—infinite repair drones—is a disastrous design choice for anyone who enjoys the "clearing out an area" satisfaction of traditional shooters.

The "Whack-a-Mole" Loop: You kill a robot, only for a drone to fix it 30 seconds later.

Inconsistent Stealth: The game demands stealth but gives you clunky tools to execute it, leading to "Alert Level" spirals that drain your ammo and patience.

Artificial Difficulty: Instead of smarter enemies, the game just makes them "bullet sponges" as you progress, turning combat into a resource-draining slog rather than a skill-based challenge.

The Ugly: The Identity Crisis
Atomic Heart doesn't know what it wants to be. It markets itself as a fast-paced action game, but it plays like a slow, punishing survival-horror game. The protagonist’s constant, aggressive bickering and the repetitive "fetch-key-to-open-door" mission structure make the mid-game feel like a literal job.

I would probably give this a mixed/neutral rating if I could.

All you need to know is this was the devs first time working on a game ever. And it shows in the jank and design choices.

There will be some frustration, but the world and lore is pretty interesting.

I want to love this game because of its unique setting, but it is a complete mess. Playing Atomic Heart feels like playing through a pastiche of every remotely popular Single Player FPS of the past 30 years (Cyberpunk, Bioshock, Resident Evil, Prey, Uncharted, etc.). 

Plot wise, there is some really interesting ideas, but its strung together in such a linear and jarring way that it feels like you're being read a children's book. Games like Bioshock are interesting narratives because you are not spoon fed the story, but rather experience it through the environment and level design. Atomic Heart felt like it wanted to have be a character drama, choices matter story, political intrigue, detail sci-fi, alternative history, and cosmic horror all at once, but managed to do none of them. 

The gameplay is decent, but the weird combination of puzzles, bullet sponge enemies, and ultra linear level design leave the second half of the game feeling like a bit of a chore. The open world felt pointless to explore because there was no way to stop enemies re-spawning for more than a couple minutes. Stealth was also non-existent, and levels were ultra linear. 

Style wise, the art and music direction is phenomenal. The setting is a fun and fresh idea. But the way the gameplay interacts with these elements makes it feel shallow.

Ultimately, this game aspires for the likes of Bioshock and Prey, but despite how much the game tries, it forgets the most important part of an immersive sim, the ability to play your own way. The game being so linear and pulling from so many different popular franchises makes it feel shallow. 

Regardless, its a fun experience, but if you're looking to fill the hole that Bioshock, Prey, or any other immersive sim has left, I don't think you'll find it here. Still probably worth it if its on a good sale. 

All that said, keen to see what the developer does next.

I wanted to write a much longer review. But I'm gonna keep it short.

In essence, the game is decent. Not amazing. Decent. The base game has a lot of issues, from gameplay, to story, to not really having a clear vision of what it wants to be.

With the final DLC, I can say that the devs have made steps in the right direction. My biggest issue with the base game is that there was a clear mismanagment of resources, and the team overextended, trying to create a weird semi-open-world, leading to a game that felt as wide as an ocean but as deep as a puddle.

The DLCs fixed that issue by being linear experiences. Which lead to much more concise and enjoyable playthroughs.

The core gameplay loop was also improved in the DLCs. Even though it still suffered from the foundation that was previously set. 

The base game was trying to be a mash of DOOM 2016 gunplay and "limited ammo" survival mechanics.  Probably trying to immitate the systems in Bioshock or Metro 2033. But it never felt right. 

This was fixed in the DLCs by showering you in ammo. Having a lot more combat encounters. And the game in general going for more of a FPS approach to gameplay. Once again, a more focused vision than the base game, and by extension, more enjoyable. 

Finally. The story. This is something that sadly was a mixed bag from start to finish. 

The writing is not great, the dialogue especially is extremely poor and characters genuinely sound like they're having completely different conversations, or like they're delusional. 

A problem that is worsened if you play the game in English. The Dubbing is terrible, I'm sorry. It's genuinely Bollywood levels of bad. Characters basically speak gibberish. Like the script was sent through 2007 Google Translate. 

Voices are desynced or delayed. Line delivery is weird and the emotion never feels right. Out of everyone Char-les and Katya I think are the only ones that are more ok. But both don't have lips or faces, so maybe it was more of an issue of trying to line up the English voice-lines to the original animations? I have no idea. Though they still suffer from those delusions I mentioned.

I ended up playing the final DLC in russian, with english subtitles because the dubbing was the worst it has ever been. 

Still didn't help the writing. It's not terrible or extremely cringe inducing, but it's not great. Once again I feel like there is a huge indecsion on what sort of tone they want to go for. Is this a retro-sci-fi noir like Bioshock, or is it a comedy? Is this a dark, serious story, or a campy saturday morning cartoon? You can have humor in dark stories, but whatever is here feels really weirdly mashed together.

The one thing that worries me is that there are a lot of moments in the Final DLC where the characters make meta jokes about the game's issues. Comments about how a factory is huge for seemingly no reason other than "we russians like things big" and how no human would ever be able to traverse through it because "it was intended to be automated". Basically the devs joking about how the factory is just a backdrop for the level design, not meant to actually serve a purpose. And a lot of other similar jokes.

Had the DLC been perfect, with the devs showing they have now mastered their craft and know what they're doing now, yeah, those jokes would be funny. Like "ha ha, remember where we started guys? And look where we are now." 

Thing is, the DLC is not perfect. The devs still have a lot of learning to do. 

Second thing, that imperfect game they're laughing about was sold at full AAA price back in 2023. This isn't a indie game where you can say "Hey, we've never made a game before, go easy on us." It's a full game, with backing from a publisher, with a full team of developers.

My point is that I hope the devs are aware of the areas their work is lacking in. The ambition and passion is there. But humility and self-awareness is something they will need to keep close moving forward. Especially with not just the sequel they're working on, but the MMO, which is a enormous task in it of itself. Which only increases my concern, because now they team might have their attention split between two projects.

After a lot of consideration, I give Atomic Heart a 7.5/10. It's decent for a first attempt. And while the base game is lacking and not worth the full price. The DLC makes the experience more complete. Moving forward, I'll be cautiously optimistic about Mundfish's future prospects. Here's hoping they take what they've learned here and make something truly great next time.

I finished the game with very mixed feelings. [b]Atomic Heart is full of contradictions[/b], which makes it hard to judge it in a clear, straightforward way.

On the one hand, the design of the dungeons is genuinely strong. From the starting area to the testing grounds with their puzzles and the later story locations, the level design is interesting and engaging. I enjoyed going through them: there is a good variety of puzzles, enemies, and combat situations.

On the other hand, all of these story locations and underground laboratories are connected by a very mediocre open world. It is not particularly memorable and mostly feels like a space you move through on your way to the actual content. If the open world were removed entirely, I honestly do not think much would change in terms of either gameplay or storytelling.

The game also has excellent weapon, robot, and environment design. The atmosphere is detailed and impressive, and there are many moments where you just want to stop and look around. Some of the scenery is genuinely beautiful. At the same time, there is also a certain awkwardness to the whole experience. It often feels like different parts of the game were made without enough coordination. For example, the soundtrack is great, but there are moments when two dialogue sequences overlap, such as a conversation with a story character playing at the same time as an audio log.

My biggest problem with the game, however, is its overall amount of content. Very early on, I got the feeling that there were not actually that many robot types or gameplay ideas in the game, and that impression stayed with me. The biggest surprise was realizing that I had completely finished the game in 27 hours. For a 60-dollar title, the gameplay side of it feels surprisingly small.

The most disappointing part is the ending. The story does not actually conclude. It simply stops somewhere in the middle of the events. As far as I understand, to see the story through, you have to buy the second and third DLCs, and even the fourth one has not been released yet. In other words, you need several paid expansions just to get what feels like the full story.

To sum it up, the game feels less like a complete standalone experience and more like several acts of a larger game sold separately. This is the first time I have seen DLC function not as extra content, but as a direct continuation that seems necessary just to finish the story.

Because of that, [b] I would not recommend buying it at full price[/b]. It may still be worth trying on a discount, but definitely not for 60 dollars.

Man, I'm kind of sad about this game. I expected something a bit more engaging and less frustrating, but it really felt a lot different than I was expecting. I had pretty high hopes here.

The beginning of the game really pulled me in. The art and graphics are incredible... huge shout out to the art team, because they nailed it. The premise of the story seemed pretty good at first too! I started to feel some bioshock vibes, but after exiting the first lab area, things really just got annoying. I gave this one an honest try and kept pushing on, but playing the game is just cumbersome.

First off, this game is a puzzle game first and foremost. Combat definitely takes a back seat to the puzzles. This wouldn't bother me if the puzzles were interesting, but they're really not. A lot of the recycled puzzles where you're rotating a floor or room are just time sinks. It takes longer to get the puzzle set up than to just move through it. Half the time, there is some weird gap in the flooring that doesn't feel like it was meant to be where you fall down. It's not hard to solve, it's just annoying.

The nail in the coffin for me was getting stuck for the 5th time in 10 hours and not being able to get unstuck. The way the save system works, it doesn't necessarily set you back far, but I was set back before one of the aforementioned crappy puzzles several times due to getting stuck on ANYTHING and EVERYTHING. Climbable walls, stairs, hand rails... you name it, I got stuck on it. Most of the time, I could dash my way out, but several times, I simply had to reload a save. Not to mention the climbing is janky as can be.

Combat doesn't feel fun and snappy like Cyberpunk. Everything works, it's not terrible, but it's just not fun. Everything feels slow and clunky, and even when you get better, everything still feels like a chore. I feel like I was missing something and I probably am, but this seems like a common critique. Then, add on the fact that in the open world, enemies constantly get healed and respawned by the flying robots that you just feel like engaging the enemy is the worst way to play. You get swarmed and the more you kill, the more just respawn and overrun you. The beginning of the game before this happens is literally the best part.

Main character is pretty cringy. Feels like a millennial edge lord wrote everything thinking "yeah what would sound the most BADASS for this guy to say while also making people laugh?" It just falls flat so much. The humor doesn't stick the landing and everything feels forced. 

Lastly, the dreaded open world scanning mechanic is here as well. Can't stand it anymore. I don't like viewing a game with such great artwork through the lens of a scanner looking for items or objectives I need. 

Could be worse for sure... I wouldn't have continued if it weren't for the art and environmental design, but frustration with everything else got the better of me. May pick it up later, but if I do, I'll follow a guide and try to find an OP build to breeze through it.

There is one thing really holding this game back: you cannot use all the DLC weapons and skills in the main game and vice versa. Please change that as it will give much more incentive to purchase the DLCs.

This game is like waking up in a Soviet utopia, only to be chased by robots gone rogue and yelled at by your talking glove who thinks it's smarter than you (it is).
The plot is chaotic, confusing, and completely unhinged, just like Mother Russia intended.
It’s like BioShock got drunk on vodka, punched Cyberpunk in the face, and then tried to juggle philosophy, communism, and slapstick horror - all while ballet dancing on hardbass.
Thus, BLYATPUNK !!
10/10 would flirt with the fridge again.

Atomic Heart is absolutely killing it with the DLCs!
Each one has been a wild ride packed with style, action, and fresh content  minus Limbo, which was kinda mid. But the rest? Pure fire. I’m beyond hyped for the 4th DLC. It feels like it’s going to be the one that ties everything together and really elevates Atomic Heart to another level.
Awesome graphics, not elden ring difficult, neither solitaire easy, enjoyable story. My life's better after playing it.

Such a disappointment. The game starts off very very well, controls are good, weapons are fun to use, and an interesting upgrade system. (SPOILERS BELOW)

However, once you escape the 1st area and get into the "open world" areas, the game takes a dive.
Why? Infinitely (and quickly) respawning enemies. You destroy a camera, a flying robot comes to fix it. Same with enemies. It takes LITERALLY less than ONE second for the flying robots to come to rebuild the cameras you break down. 
If you kill the flying robots before they reach the cameras? THEY JUST KEEP RESPAWNING.

They basically built a beautiful open area, THEORETICALLY inviting you to explore and roam, however made the game so hostile towards the player that you give up on exploring, the constant and nonstop respawning goes diametrically against the exploration and wandering around.
You run out of patience, and avoid all other buildings (which contains blueprints) because the game makes its damnedest sure to make enemies annoying as possible, all the time, everywhere.

After seeing the open world area, I would've preferred to be stuck in corridors in the complex, where there was no infinitely respawning enemies.

And if the objetctive of this design is just to make you run away from everything....why have open areas in the first place?

I think this is the first game I have ever played that is actively designed to make you NOT want to explore its world.

And that's the worst part. IT was a great great game until it opened up. Such a downfall.

I think the Art direction and atmosphere are the majority of what carries this game to a Mostly Positive. The re imagining of Soviet Russia into a Bio-shock-esque wonderland is great and what carried me through the game where the dialogue, story, and repetitive game play tried to force me away (something, something, horny fridge). I got to the end due to sunk cost fallacy, but was a struggle for the last push. So credit where its due, but do not recommend.

I feel that if they had simply lowered the dialogue during the early and middle of the stages of the game and improved the combat, this game would be fantastic. For a game of this magnitude for a company and development team so new to games, it is genuinely quite impressive and overall, I did enjoy it.

Likes:

- The story setting and theme.
- Game optimisation.
- Enemy variety (I am impressed).
- Fridge lady.
- Terekshova
- Soviet Granny.
- Perk trees.
- Door unlocking puzzles.
- Visuals.

Dislikes:

- The main character talks too much. This takes away from the story as I sometimes feel that less is more. As someone playing this game subbed, too much dialogue happens during fight scenes which means I miss it.
- The gunplay and glove abililities are a bit weak, even with upgrades. I wish when you made contact with shots or a melee weapon, it had more pop and more damage was visibile.
- Having to respec part of your character for certain boss battles.
- At times the game can feel a bit boring and empty. It would have been better to see more living people throughout the story, even if some of them die shortly afterwards. Certain areas to feel less open and for exploration (others may disagree, but open world games get a bit samey these days).
- The flying robots that repair destroyed enemies. Get rid of this rubbish. Especially in the outside areas where you want to explore but can't.
- Too many individual boss fights for my liking. I do enjoy the challenge they present, but after a while you get a bit sick and tired of having to respec your characters and then fighting them.
- This game would have benefited from being a little shorter in terms of story length.
a refrigerator sexually harassed me about an hour into the game

Recommended but kinda barely. Its really weird and strange but in a slightly more bad way than a good way. If you can get it fairly cheap go for it. I paid $18 Gold edition which has all 4 expansions. 

If youre looking for more of a Bioshock type of game like me you may come away a little disappointed. Its close but man this game has some good ideas but also does a lot of weird, bizarre and/or annoying stuff that really hurts it or doesnt fit in very well, for me at least. 

Things i liked:
-Graphics and areas are really nice to look at. Nice artwork, interesting looking game. 
-Hardly any loading screens. Theres a few sections where the game is clearly loading but its very few. The only time i got a loading screen is first boot and if you die. It ran pretty well too and looks nice and detailed with lots of sharpening, upscaling options. Not to mention an accessibility menu so you can tweak highlighting enemies, intractable objects, etc. Thank you devs, just next time make it glow instead of a solid yellow color. 
-Shooting felt pretty good as does the melee combat...after a few upgrades. Melee combat pretty good too...after a few upgrades. 
-The [Bioshock] powers you get are fun to use. I just stuck with Mass Telekinesis. Lifting 4 or 5 dudes up then slamming them on the ground felt great and was a ton of fun (however devs- we need more intense sound effects and better dismemberment please include for sequel). 
-You can freely buy and refund weapons as you wish without any penalty to find what you like the best (i stuck with the laser pistol, shotgun, fatboy rocket launcher and the assault rifle).
-Decent supporting cast. 
-15 hour-ish single player campaign with dlc that will explain more to set up the sequel. Ive only finished Enchantment Under the Sea and it felt like a big step forward in the right direction.

Things i hated:
-The main protagonist is arrogant, obnoxious and kind of a jerk. Reminded me of the original Ratchet & Clank on PS2 where Ratchet gets turned into a jerk most of the game, (later made much more likeable in future games though). "Crispy Critters" catch phrase is sorta lame and cringy and he says it way too much. He came across as very unlikable, (however in enhancement under the sea DLC he is much more likeable and hardly cusses which was refreshing, so maybe the devs are fixing criticism and a better insight of the announced sequel.
-The dialogue in this game is just....weird. Its really difficult for me to describe, but it just irritated me a lot of the time. Its just bizarre. Same with some cinematics. 
-Bosses are so fast and twitchy. You also get knocked down way too much throughout the game.
-The open world section doesnt cut it for me. The map feels so cumbersome to use. I avoided every single optional area because it was so annoying. And if i DID stumble across one it brickwalls you with a key which you have to climb a thing and yeah this game does a lot of that throughout missions come to think of it as well. Also no compass and no minimap. 
-The whole vibe of the game screams it wants to be in an eerie unknown world like Bioshock games but it throws so much weird dialogue and bizarre this and that and following just the main story was in exercise in frustration trying to understand some of the stuff happening. I mean i like weird games but this one is just everything being thrown at you all at once- You got Grandma with tons of guns with a flying house that shoots flames. Then there's what felt like a 
[i] forever [/i]  length of a cutscene where a female robot that sticks its hand into another robots stomach, removes a metal rod which then turns into 2 pieces, then they attach to themselves to...unlock a door. Limbo sections where youre a furry creature collecting apples in la-la land. The weapons and upgrade vending machine is an overly horny female voice, and the song that plays when its open i HATE IT. Bizarre stuff is just constantly happening here, there, everywhere all the time and its weird. Too weird. There's good weird and bad weird and most of this falls into bad weird, for me at least. 
-Music. I think ive read theres 3 music composers, one of which is Mick Gordon from the Doom reboot. Yes it shows. Felt like i was playing that game. But then theres music that sounds like a kindergarten rhyme-with-me music. Then theres some orchestral stuff. All thrown in without any regard for the location. It doesnt make for any strong vibe it just made the game more fractured and kills the atmosphere. 
-Upgrade/weapons menu is a chore to use. Not only that, but the one song that plays while youre trying to figure out what to upgrade is just irritating. There's also an annoying animation you have to watch before actually getting to use your weapon, (same with door locks, just make it fall to the ground like Bioshock Infinite). 

I recommend starting on easy, then move up as you go if you want. I also turned on auto-heal which is super helpful qol feature. About 6 hours in i also turned off QTE and and later turned on auto puzzle solve because of all the many door locks.

Looking forward to the sequel. Hopefully it improves/fixes things about this game.

cons :

Is this the greatest game of all time? No. Are the "open world" segments a drag? Yes. However, the story is good, the combat is fun, the lore is great, and the game runs pretty dang well on release. That is a win in my book and it is worth a play-through for sure!

Actually polished game in 2023, yeah crazy I know.
From the first 3 hours of my playtime the game is absolutely gorgeous, plays really well and is well optimised.

Atomic heart is a game with some great strengths and is at times quite a lot of fun... but it's also a game that feels frustratingly half-a$$ed and unfinished.


Pros:
The art and design of the world is great for the most part.

The worldbuilding is well executed and most parts of the universe the game exists in feel very well thought out.

Most of the gameplay is quite fun, although less so when you run into the less complete parts of the game.

A lot of the voice actors do a really good job... with what they're given.


Cons:
Where to even begin, there's quite a lot wrong with the game. There's a reason all the pros came with a "but".

The game contains a small amount of AI generated art in it, only like 0.01% of it but it's very baffling since the rest of the game looks so great and 2023 AI art is so obvious and crappy looking to boot. 
There's one mosaic texture you can see near the end of the opening section of the game that looks like complete garbage surrounded by beautifully handcrafted environments, who thought this was a good corner to cut?

While the worldbuilding is good, the dialog goes from mediocre to downright bad. So overall the writing leaves a pretty bad impression.
The main character spouts a lot of sarcastic tough guy talk but at the same time also whines like an annoying kid all the time in the dialog with other characters.
Every robot character speaks in sexual innuendo constantly, especially annoying is the vending machine where you upgrade your weapons and craft things, it just never lets up.

Even the worldbuilding isn't without flaws however because the creators of the game clearly had no love for the music of the 1950s so unlike in Fallout where all music fit a single era, in this game there's a quantum radio that plays music from "possible futures." leading to the game, the further it goes along being filled with more and more modern house music and stuff, not just in background music but even on location based radios and such.

While there isn't that many female characters, all except Granny Zina (who is your classic babushka,) look extremely modern, nothing retro about them, not even the haircuts feel older than the last few years, very odd.

The game being open world was clearly an afterthought. In the optional dungeons you can meet bosses before they are introduced in the main plot, yet the dialog about them is still there when you meet them in the main plot, not the first time you meet them. There's also a character that gets killed partway through the story and if you go to a part further back on the map you can still get radioed by him because you had yet to trigger that call.
Some areas in the open world section feel strangely empty, like they placed the buildings and debris and such but didn't add any loot, lore, nor hardly even enemies.
The optional dungeons have a lot of regular loot right at the start and then almost none besides the blueprints, (which are the reason you go there,) so there's not much encouragement to explore them even when they don't look completely linear which is a missed opportunity. Since there's zero lore stuff in the optional dungeons they don't really feel like they're a part of the world.

Due mostly to the open world section the dosing out of worldbuilding/lore is really uneven, besides the optional dungeons having nothing at all, near the end of the game you get to an archive where you'll spend ages reading lore if you're interested, seems like it should have been sprinkled throughout the game more evenly.

Parts of the game are pretty unbalanced like enemies that can mob up on you so you can't move, doesn't happen too often but always frustrating when it does. Bosses that can stun lock you and hit you multiple times in a row without you being able to heal or move in between, which is a big problem if a boss takes almost half your healthbar per hit.

TLDR; It's not a bad game, but it's not worth the hype nor the full price. The story execution is mid at best, the english voice acting is rough and the gameplay is repetitive. Outside of its premise and visuals, there's nothing special to it. Get it on sale if you really want it. 

If you really want to get this game, get it on sale because it's definitely not worth the full price. The score and the art direction is nice, but it falls short on everything else. While the premise is interesting, the story is poorly executed and there's no feeling of resolution to either endings (if anything, the endings, for me, knocked the game down to a 4/10 at best). The game entirely relies on near incessant info dumping to convey its story and its world, and it does very little to make Atomic Heart's universe feel more alive or immersive. It gets tiring fast both on account of the amount of information being thrown at you and the english voice acting. Said voice acting is [i] at best [/i] middle of the road. Conversations feel stiff and unnatural, which I guess does go with the characters— they all feel rather bland. The main character only stands out because of how annoying he comes off across. Outside of that, he very much just feels like your generic action shooter protagonist. 

The gameplay gets boring and repetitive fast. Most of the game involves searching and retrieving something, with a few different puzzles and some combat in-between. There's very little variation in the puzzles and while they do show up here and there, it's definitely not enough for this game to have the puzzle tag attached to it. The combat is fairly alright, but again, very run of the mill at best. At worst, it gets annoying when there are repair robots in the area, and even worse when facing the Plyush type enemies, which become repetitive bosses in a few sections. There are few boss fights in the game, but none of them feel particularly fun or rewarding. 

And for a game claiming to be open world, exploring doesn't feel rewarding either. Outside of the testing grounds, there's no real incentive to explore, except maybe a few computers where you can read some emails. 

All in all, Atomic Heart had a lot of potential, but it fell short on too many aspects for me to recommend the game at that price point (or frankly, at all). Once the novelty of its visuals wear off, it very quickly starts feeling exhausting. It's especially disappointing, for me. I don't usually write reviews, but this was one of the games I was most looking forward to. My mistake was coming in with high expectations, something that felt justified with all the positive reviews. I should have lowered said expectations, because for a full-priced game, I was expecting a lot more than what I got. While it has its highs, it also has a lot of lows which, for me, really outweighed the good. Again, for a game selling at an AAA game price, its quality doesn't reflect that. If you're willing to buy the game at full price, all the more power to you, but nothing in Atomic Heart justifies that price point.

Awesome idea, awesome world, awesome graphics, and much more. Atomic Heart has a lot going for it. The setting is genuinely interesting, the visuals are fantastic, and even the story had a lot of potential.

And that's probably what makes my experience with the game so frustrating. I actually found the story interesting. There were a lot of things I wanted to know more about, but the way the story was presented to the player often felt too vague and fragmented. Important information was scattered around, hinted at, or buried in conversations and logs, and I often felt like I was missing pieces of the bigger picture. The story itself was cool, but I don't think it was presented in a way that made me care about it as much as I could have.

The biggest problem for me was the repetitiveness. After a while, it felt like I was doing the same things over and over again, and it completely killed my motivation to keep playing. What started as an interesting and exciting experience eventually became a chore.

The soundtrack didn't help either. It was all over the place. One moment it's a beautiful russian lullaby, then some classic Soviet music, and suddenly there's D&B or hard rock blasting in the background. Don't get me wrong, some of those tracks were absolute bangers, but they often felt completely out of place. Instead of enhancing the atmosphere, they sometimes completely killed the immersion.

It's a shame, because there's a really cool game buried underneath all of this. The world, art direction, graphics, and overall concept are genuinely awesome. But for me, the repetitive gameplay eventually outweighed all of those positives.

I genuinely liked this one. While some parts did not appeal to my (current) interests in gaming (sick of open worlds, not really interested in first-person shooters either, actually), the game did well in making me still feel welcome: lower difficulty, QTEs can be disabled, the open world is actually quite small and can be traversed quickly via vehicles or on foot and even the annoying floating quest marker can be disabled very easily with a small mod.

The most interesting parts of the game were its story, which was as good of an homage to Bioshock as we can probably expect. Yes, indeed, I like the story. The atmosphere and world building is quite a sight as well. But most importantly, and maybe a bit surprisingly, the most fun I had was in the optional underground research labs. Almost devoid of combat, but decent puzzles with some first-person jumping thrown in for good measure. It could have been boring and clunky, but it wasn't -- I had so much fun in them that after the first one I basically did all eight of them in order, even though I wasn't interested in some of those gun upgrades.

Overall the base game was really much better than I thought it would be. Granted, I didn't play it for its gunplay or challenge, so players looking for either of those probably have a different opinion. I played it for its style, atmosphere and story and had a good time with that.

Since I also bought the 3rd DLC (the other two are apparently either irrelevant to the canon story or hot garbage), I will be playing that as well. But just speaking about the base game, I recommend it.

I was very and very skeptical about this game, considering how long it was in development and the accompanying articles that everything was going very badly. It seemed like another scam project that would be done half-heartedly just to make money. I'm very glad that I was very wrong about that.

There aren't too many AAA projects from the CIS [i](Commonwealth of Independent States)[/i] segment, unfortunately [i](free-to-play trash doesn't count)[/i], so I'm genuinely happy that the game has been successful.

It's truly a high-tech project, with no loading screens between locations, fantastic visuals, beautiful animations, and functional interactivity. It's not without its quirks, but overall, it didn't strain my eyes too much.

I thougth I never felt nostalgic for the USSR and Soviet romanticism, but the opening scene drew me in for two hours. I was captivated by the posters, engaged in conversations, listened to dialogues, and admired the visuals and set design. I experienced familiar yet simultaneously new emotions.

Throughout the entire game, it's fascinating to observe the evolution of the main character and relationship with "AI" companion. The humor, comments, and their interactions with each other were enjoyable and conducive to empathy. Almost every event comes with a corresponding comment and assessment.

In terms of gameplay, the game strongly resembles the first BioShock. Melee attacks, shooting, and [strike]plasmids[/strike]abilities are okay, but sometimes, there's a sense of "roughness." However, over 32 hours in the main game, I never felt that shooting became boring. The weapon arsenal may not be extensive, but it was more than sufficient for me, plus the upgrades.

However, toward the end of the game, I realized I didn't want to use weapons again just to trigger another wave of enemies in the open world, which is probably the biggest and most annoying downside. You simply can't explore all the areas and collect materials because enemies start swarming you. Greetings to the rooftop at Testing Ground 6, where I had to destroy enemies whose respawn point got stuck next to a computer for cameras. I spent 20 minutes trying to open that damned door [i](by the way, the marker for the camera also glitched, and I couldn't get to it on the map)[/i], and in the end, I gave up and reloaded to carefully replay that part.

Since I started talking about the downsides, the open world lacks content. The beginning is very solid and rich with diaries and content. But once you get into the open world, there's not much except beautifully designed locations [i](the aesthetics of Soviet "retro-futurism" are outstanding)[/i]. There are Testing Ground challenges that you have to complete to unlock upgrades, and that's all. Maybe there are some interesting locations, but because of the respawning enemies, I didn't want to roam in circles to check that. Most of the time, I found just resources. That moment when you break into yet another cabin to find diaries, but all you find is another pile of resources.

Did anyone even understand the map? I didn't. It's just functional.

But again, I never believed that this game would work. The open world and the game world, in general, function as they should, even though it really annoyed me at times. Points of interest are always well-furnished, and there's always something interesting to explore. Story-related locations, in particular, earned my respect.

I also liked that spent resources and development points can always be retrieved without any additional actions. So, closer to the 2/3 mark of the game, I didn't have to loot crates anymore (on medium difficulty). I could experiment and play as much as I wanted.

The story turned out to be far less straightforward than I thought based on the trailers. That's undoubtedly a plus. In some moments, it may seem somewhat naive, but by the end of the game, you're the only one who feels naive [i](well, at least me)[/i].

For me, Atomic Heart was a pleasant surprise in 2023. Perhaps my zero expectations for the game contributed to that. But I was impressed. So, thumbs up.

Atomic Heart is one of the most unique FPS games I’ve played in a long time. The alternate-history Soviet setting is absolutely stunning — the retro-futuristic world is full of weird, beautiful, and creepy details that make exploration a real treat.

Combat feels great. You get a satisfying mix of guns, melee weapons, and crazy glove powers that let you freeze, shock, or toss enemies around. It’s fast, chaotic, and really fun once you get the hang of it.

The enemy design is wild — creepy robots, weird mutants, and intense boss fights keep things fresh. Also, the soundtrack SLAPS. Perfect mix of eerie ambient sounds and energetic battle music.

Sure, the story gets a bit weird at times, but it’s actually pretty deep and thought-provoking if you pay attention. It’s got that BioShock meets Soviet sci-fi vibe.

If you’re into shooters with strong style, solid combat, and a weird (in a good way) world to explore, Atomic Heart is absolutely worth it.

Maybe my mind will change here, but as of right now, I spent money on this and haven't wanted to touch it since. I was playing and trudging along (spent hours stuck in a limbo of combat), thinking it will certainly get better eventually. Alas, no. I just could not get over how janky it is. I don't know if it was trying to do or be too many things at once, but there's a lot of QoL that's lacking and cheapens the experience. It's also wildly repetitive. It's fun to kill robots for a little while, but the decision to keep them repairing continuously, non-stop, and then letting the player know that sometimes it's better to not engage - what other option is there? There is no stealth. You cannot annihilate an area for some peace, because the repair bots are there before you even finished off the enemies. You fight, or you run until you are inundated with 50 enemies on you. You get mere seconds to enjoy the atmosphere and the cool world they built. There were definitely better ways to do this without making it feel like a never-ending nightmare. I just expected a cleaner experience with invigorating gameplay, driven by a story. The "dungeons"/bunkers for upgrades are tedious and so much of what you're doing, you'll do 10 more times in the next area. I love the idea of the world this is set in, I love the concept, and I love the look. Everything's really cool in that regard, but you get dropped in and feel like you must have missed something right out of the gate. Heck, the path forward 90% of the time involves jumping or dropping or maneuvering to an area that looks like it would be out of bounds, off limits, or not the intended pathway forward. Good games gently guide the player along a path, while finding ways to nudge them back to the correct path if they seem lost or are not progressing. Something like a companion or NPC making a radio call after 5 minutes reminding your objective, the player character remarking on what seems to be the way around an obstacle, or even some debris falling or something in the environment to help force a player to look at and consider a certain direction. If you play Atomic Heart, you'll see exactly what I mean. It's not about hand-holding, no one's asking for that. It's about game design. I intend to finish the game some day, and maybe my mind will change when I do, but as of right now, I haven't wanted to bother. TLDR; a great vision not fully realized. It works in some areas while under-serving anything but repetitive combat in most others. It sometimes feels as though one game was being developed, then scrapped for another while keeping a majority of the components of the original vision.

Atomic Heart is one of those games where the focus isn’t on breaking down every small flaw, but on understanding the overall experience it delivers. And in that sense, it does its job very well. From the start, what stands out is the world itself. 
There’s a strong identity here, especially in how it blends retro-futuristic technology with a Soviet-inspired setting. For players familiar with games like Fallout universe, there’s an immediate sense of familiarity in the concept: a highly advanced world, shaped by a different ideological direction, with its own technological evolution. It’s not the same thing, but the inspiration is clearly there.

The game builds its narrative in a way that starts slightly vague, but gradually becomes more engaging as you progress. It doesn’t throw everything at you immediately, instead it creates curiosity, encouraging exploration and slowly revealing what is happening in the world. That sense of mystery, combined with the atmosphere, is one of its strongest aspects.
In terms of gameplay, Atomic Heart remains consistent. It doesn’t try to overcomplicate things, and more importantly, it doesn’t get in the way of the experience. The combat, weapons, and abilities feel modern and responsive, and overall the game maintains a good balance between action and progression. This is not a game where I felt the need to constantly question its mechanics, it simply works.

That said, there are small aspects that could have been handled better. One of the most noticeable is the crafting system, particularly when using the Nora machine. Crafting items one by one, with repeated animations and no option to batch craft efficiently, becomes tedious over time and breaks the pacing, especially when you just want to quickly prepare and move on.
Boss fights are another area that feels less refined compared to the rest of the experience. While visually impressive, they often lack mechanical depth, relying more on endurance than on dynamic interaction. Movement during these encounters also feels slightly limited, making dodging less effective than it should be, which can turn some fights into more of a forced exchange rather than a skill-based encounter.

Despite these issues, they don’t significantly harm the overall experience. Atomic Heart remains a game that is enjoyable from start to finish, with a strong identity and a clear vision of what it wants to be.

In the end, this is a game that delivers a solid and engaging experience without trying to be something it isn’t. It respects its own concept, maintains consistency throughout, and offers a world that is worth exploring. If you enjoy games with strong atmosphere and a sense of curiosity, especially if you appreciate titles like Fallout, this is definitely worth experiencing.

[b] Atomic Heart [/b] can be described as a budget version of Cyberpunk 2077, as the atmosphere is definitely there, but the limitations of the developers in terms of budget and storytelling are clearly visible. On top of that, the game got caught up in political controversies, which led to harsher reviews from critics. As a result, it lost many potential players and, with them, a significant part of its potential profit.

Despite this, Atomic Heart is a game full of contrasts, where its strong points make up for some of its flaws. One of the biggest drawbacks is the lack of teleportation and a limited open world that doesn't encourage exploration due to the absence of side quests or extra elements to discover. The main missions are rather simple and lead the player by the hand, but this is balanced by challenging logic puzzles. These puzzles can be frustrating at times, but solving them is very satisfying.

A big advantage of the game is its unique style, set in an alternate Soviet reality. Both the machines and the cities shown in cutscenes impress with their detailed design, creating a very atmospheric world. Unfortunately, other locations, where players spend most of their time, feel empty and generic, lacking any special features to stand out. Another highlight is the excellent Polish localization, which was a very pleasant surprise and significantly improved my experience.

The developers are also actively supporting the game by regularly adding new expansions, which expand the world of Atomic Heart and provide additional hours of gameplay. Despite its flaws, the game is an interesting experience that's definitely worth checking out.

[h1]Introduction[/h1]
A first-person shooter set in the USSR in the years following World War 2, Russia has become a technological dystopia where advanced machines are completing a wide range of tasks for humans. Atomic Heart attempts to reinvent what games like Prey and Bioshock did in a new environment and setting. But did their formula start the reaction they were hoping for or did the experiment blow up in their faces?
